questions.qtext:
Consider the relational scheme $\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}, \mathrm{E}, \mathrm{F}, \mathrm{G}, \mathrm{H})$ and the following functional dependencies over $$\mathrm{R} : \mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{BCD} ; \mathrm{AD} \rightarrow \mathrm{E} ; \mathrm{EFG} \rightarrow \mathrm{H} ; \mathrm{F} \rightarrow \mathrm{GH}$$

Based on these functional dependencies, there is one key for $\mathrm{R}$. One of these four functional dependencies can be removed without altering the key. Which one?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 1)
Answer is option $\boxed{\text{C. EFG} \to H}$

R(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H)

FD:
$$
\{ A \rightarrow BCD,\; AD \rightarrow E,\; EFG \rightarrow H,\; F \rightarrow GH \}
$$

Candidate key: $AF^+ = ABCDEFGH \;\checkmark$

1) Lets remove $\{A \rightarrow BCD\}$ and check if $AF$ is still CK.

$$
AF^+ = AFGH \;\times
$$

We cant remove this FD.

2) Lets remove $\{AD \rightarrow E\}$

$$
AF^+ = AFBCDGH \;\times
$$

We can't remove this functional dependency.

3) Lets remove $\{EFG \rightarrow H\}$

$$
AF^+ = AFBCDEGH \;\checkmark
$$

We can remove this FD.

4) Lets remove $\{F \rightarrow GH\}$

$$
AF^+ = AFBCDE \;\times
$$

We can't remove this FD.

questions.qtext:
Consider the relation $\mathbf{R}(\underline{\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}}, \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D}, \mathbf{E}, \mathbf{F})$ with $\{\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}\}$ as a composite primary key and the following dependencies:

  • $\{\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}\} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}, \mathrm{E}, \mathrm{F}$
  • $\mathrm{E} \rightarrow \mathrm{D}$
  • $\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{F}$

Which of the following options are true? (Select all correct choices)
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 1)

Since every relation is in 1NF, here we'll start checking for 2NF and look if we find a 2NF violation:

According to 2NF,

Every Non-prime attribute is fully dependent on every candidate key ( No partial dependency should exist).

Thus, any dependency of the sort:

Some proper subset of C.K ------> Non-Prime attribute should not exist.

In this relation, the Candidate Key is AB, and the three dependencies do not violate 2NF. Thus, the above relation is in 2NF.

3NF violation:

Nonprime ----> Non-prime is a violation of 3NF, and we see that dependencies are satisfying this. Thus, the above relation is not in 3NF.

Thus, options B,C,D are the answers.

questions.qtext:
Suppose $R$ and $S$ are two relations. Let $C$ be the referential integrity constraint that says: whenever $R$ has a tuple with some values $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ in particular attributes $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$, there must be a tuple of $S$ that has the same values $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ in particular attributes $B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n$.

Which of the following operations on $R, S$ can cause violation of the constraint $\mathrm{C}?$
questions.solution:
Answer: A, D

Selected solution (score: 4)

Answer is option $\boxed{A,D}$

Since relation $R$ refers to $S$, so, if we delete a tuple from $R$, it doesn’t cause referential integrity violation.

According to refrential integrity constraint , The values in the attributes of $R$ either can be null or a value already present in the corresponding $S$

A. Insert in R can cause violation because what if the value is not present in S.

B. Insert in S will not cause violation.

C. Delete from R will not cause violation.

D. Delete from S will cause a problem because what is the value is being used by R.

questions.qtext: Which one of the following statements about normal forms is $\text{FALSE}?$

options.text: Lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition into $\text{3NF}$ is always possible
Lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition into $\text{BCNF}$ is always possible
Any relation with two attributes is in $\text{BCNF}$

questions.solution:
Answer: C, A

Selected solution (score: 6)

Answer is option $\boxed{C}$

A. Yes true, BCNF is stricter than 3NF. Refer the diagram below. Hence True

B. 3NF synthesis Algorithm guarantees lossless dependency preserving decomposition. Hence True.

C. BCNF decomposition might or might not be dependency preserving but it is always lossless. Hence False.

D. Any relation in $2$ Attribute is always in BCNF.

Let the relation be $R(A,B)$ Now for FDs there are only $3$ possibilties.

Case 1:

FD = { $A \rightarrow B$, $B \rightarrow A$ }

Since R has only 2 attributes. Therefore both A and B here will form a candidate key.

This Relation is in BCNF.

--------------------------------------------------

Case 2:

FD = { $A \rightarrow B$ }

Here only A is candidate key.

This Relation is also in BCNF.

--------------------------------------------------

Case 3:

FD = { }

That is no Functional Dependency in FD set.

NO candidate key Here.

This is also in BCNF.

Hence True

questions.qtext:
Consider the functional dependencies (FDs) of a relation $\mathrm{R}$ and below-mentioned properties:

  • $\text{P1:}$ A non-prime attribute determines a different non-prime attribute.
  • $\text{P2:}$ A proper subset of a candidate key determines a non-prime attribute.

Choose the correct option:

options.text: If some FD of $\mathrm{R}$ has property $\mathrm{P} 1, \mathrm{R}$ can't be in $2 \mathrm{NF}$
If some FD of $\mathrm{R}$ has property $\mathrm{P} 2, \mathrm{R}$ can't be in $2 \mathrm{NF}$
If some FD of $\mathrm{R}$ has property $\mathrm{P} 2, \mathrm{R}$ can still be in $2 \mathrm{NF}$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 0)

Answer is option $\boxed{B}$

If some relation has Property $P1$ then it can't be in $3NF$ . Because its a violation of $3NF$

Poperty P2 is violation of $2NF$. So if a relation has property P2 then it can't be in $2NF$.

A. If some FD of R has property P1,R can't be in 2NF.

This statement is False because there is relation possible which is not in 3NF but are in 2NF.

B. If some FD of R has property P2,R can't be in 2NF

This is True because P2 is a violation of 2NF.

C. P1 and P2 won't affect R being in 2NF.

This is False. As seen previously P2 is a violation of 2NF.

D. If some FD of R has property P2,R can still be in 2NF

Again this is False. Because P2 is a violation of 2NF

questions.qtext:
Following table has two attributes Employee_id and Manager_id, where Employee_id is a primary key and manager_id is a foreign key referencing Employee_id with on-delete cascade:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Employee_id} & \text{Manager_id} \\ \hline 20 & 40 \\ \hline 25 & 40 \\ \hline 30 & 35 \\ \hline 35 & 20 \\ \hline 40 & 45 \\ \hline 45 & 25 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

On deleting the table $(20,40)$, the set of other tuples that must be deleted to maintain the referential integrity of table is
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 3)
Given, Manager_id refers Employee_id and (20, 40) deleted.

Since Employee_id = 20 deleted, all records with Manager_id = 20 must be deleted.

So, (35, 20) must be deleted.

Since Employee_id = 35 deleted, all records with Manager_id = 35 must be deleted.

So, (30, 35) must be deleted.

And no Manager_id equals 30, so stop.

ANSWER : B

questions.qtext:
Consider the following relational schema and set of functional dependencies.

$\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}, \mathrm{E})$ with functional dependencies $\mathrm{ABC} \rightarrow \mathrm{D} ; \mathrm{CD} \rightarrow \mathrm{A} ; \mathrm{AD} \rightarrow \mathrm{E}$.

Which of the following is true?

options.text: $\mathrm{R}$ is in $3 \mathrm{NF}$ but not in BCNF.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 39)

So for the given Relation R(A, B, C, D, E),

Candidate keys are: ABC and BCD

Prime attribute: A, B, C, D

Non-prime attribute: E

To check whether the given relation is in 2NF or not we are checking for

proper subset of candidate key ->Non prime attribute(This type of FDs are violation of 2NF)

Closure of proper subset of candidate key: A*={A}, B*={B}, c*={C}, D*={D}, AB*={A,B}, AC*={A,C}, BC*={B,C},

CD*={C,D,A,E} , BD*={B,D}

Here CD is a proper subset of CK BCD and CD determines E(Non-prime Attribute)(CD->E) which is a violation of 2NF.

So, the Answer is A.

Note: To check whether the given relation is in 2NF,3NF we have to check FD closure not only given FDs.

questions.qtext:
An attribute $A$ is called prime if $A$ is in any of the candidate keys. Assume in the following statements, $\mathrm{A}$ is an attribute $\&\;\mathcal{X}$ is a set of attributes.

Consider the following statements:

  1. Domain of each attribute is an elementary type; that is, not a set or a record structure.
  2. Whenever $\mathcal{X} \mapsto A$ is a functional dependency that holds in relation $\mathbf{R}$ and $A otin \mathcal{X}$, then either
    • $A$ is prime, or
    • $\quad \mathcal{X}$ is a key or a super-key for $\mathbf{R}$.
  3. Whenever $\mathcal{X} \mapsto A$ is a functional dependency that holds in relation $\mathbf{R}$ and $A otin \mathcal{X}$, then either
    • $A$ is prime, or
    • $\mathcal{X}$ is not a proper subset of any key for $\mathbf{R}$.
  4. Whenever $\mathcal{X} \mapsto A$ is a functional dependency that holds in relation $\mathbf{R}$ and $A otin \mathcal{X}$, then
    • $\mathcal{X}$ is a key or a super-key for $\mathbf{R}$.

Which of the following is a correct match??
questions.solution:
Answer: C, A

Selected solution (score: 6)
Answer is option $\boxed{C}$

(A)

Its talking about $1NF$.

--------------------------------------------------

(B)

$X \rightarrow A$

Here, either

1) $A$ is prime, so here $X \rightarrow A$ can be of type

(i) $C_k \rightarrow prime$ $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF
(ii) $prime \rightarrow prime$ $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF

or

2) $X$ is $C_k$ or $S_k$, so here $X \rightarrow A$ can be of type

(i) $C_k \rightarrow prime$ $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF
(ii) $C_k \rightarrow non\text{-}prime$ $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF

So B is in 3NF (basically the cases don’t provide any counter eg).

--------------------------------------------------

(C)

$X \rightarrow A$

Here, either

1) $A$ is prime, so here $X \rightarrow A$ can be of type

(i) $C_k \rightarrow prime$ $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF
(ii) $prime \rightarrow prime$ $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF

or

2) $X$ is not proper subset of any key of $R$,

so here $X$ is either non prime, then $X \rightarrow A$ can be of type

(i) $nonprime \rightarrow nonprime $ only $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF violation!!!

or

$X$ is candidate key itself

(i) $C_k \rightarrow prime$ $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF
(ii) $C_k \rightarrow non\text{-}prime$ $\Rightarrow$ in 3NF

So C is not in 3NF, BUT is in 2NF.
